topic.title: Hidden Markov Models and Latent Temporal Regimes
topic.overview: Hidden Markov models explain sequences through unobserved states that evolve over time and generate observations. This topic studies learning the number and structure of states, efficient inference, flexible durations, and switching models with richer dynamics. The goal is to recover useful temporal organization without directly observing the underlying regimes.
topic.whyItMatters: Latent states can summarize recurring conditions, but different parameterizations may produce similar observations. Identifiability, duration assumptions, and inference approximations therefore matter for interpretation. When regimes have different causal relationships, recovering transitions alone is not enough to establish the structure within each regime.
topic.evolution: A 1992 Bayesian model-merging method learns HMM topology by progressively combining states. Subsequent work develops large-state inference, nonlinear embedded models, and nonparametric alternatives. In 2026, a switching-model study establishes identifiability under specified nonlinear, instantaneous, and exponential-family noise assumptions, while another representative extends duration modeling to depend on observations.
openQuestions: How can inferred states be distinguished from artifacts of emission or duration assumptions?
Which temporal measurements identify regime-specific structure when switching is frequent?
